4.1.m: Homage to glorious Gaṇeśa.
We venerate that great lord, the beloved child of Maheśāna,
Gaṇeśa, whose face is like the leader of elephants, free from all affliction. (1)

4.1.s: bhūmiṣṭhāpi na yātrabhūstridivatopyuccairadhaḥsthāpi yā yā baddhā bhuvi muktidāsyuramṛtaṃ yasyāṃ mṛtā jaṃtavaḥ ..
4.1.d: भूमिष्ठापि न यात्रभूस्त्रिदिवतोप्युच्चैरधःस्थापि या या बद्धा भुवि मुक्तिदास्युरमृतं यस्यां मृता जंतवः ..
4.1.m: Though standing on earth, it is not part of this world; though situated below, it is higher than heaven; / though bound to the earth, it grants liberation; and creatures who die in it become immortal.

4.1.s: yā nityaṃ trijagatpavitrataṭinī tīre suraiḥ sevyate sā kāśī tripurārirājanagarī pāyādapāyājjagat .. 2 ..
4.1.d: या नित्यं त्रिजगत्पवित्रतटिनी तीरे सुरैः सेव्यते सा काशी त्रिपुरारिराजनगरी पायादपायाज्जगत् .. 2 ..
4.1.m: It is constantly served by the gods on the bank of the river that purifies the three worlds: / may that Kāśī, the royal city of Tripura's foe, protect the universe from calamity! (2)
Homage to that Maheśa, on the pretext of the three twilights,
before whom the lords of the three worlds constantly come and go. (3)
The author of the eighteen Purāṇas, the son of Satyavatī,
narrated this tale that removes sin before Sūta. (4)
Glorious Vyāsa said:
Once the illustrious Nārada, having bathed in the waters of the glorious Narmadā
and worshiped the glorious Oṃkāra, who gives everything to all embodied beings, (5)
as he walked, beheld before him the Vindhya mountain,
which removes the distress of worldly existence and is adorned by the waters of the Revā, (6)
making this earth—both in its stationary form and its moving form—
truly merit its name of 'possessor of wealth' (vasumatī) by virtue of its abundant splendor: (7)
an abode of sweetness with mango trees, dispelling sorrow with aśoka trees,
adorned everywhere with palmyra, tamāla, hintāla, and sāla trees; (8)
resembling an aerial city with its betel-nut trees, truly blessed with bilva fruits,
endowed with great beauty by its agallochum trees, tawny like monkeys with monkey-fruit trees; (9)
charming with lakuca fruits resembling the breasts of the forest's beauty,
illuminated by plantain trees providing fruits sweet as nectar; (10)
displaying beauty like a courtly pavilion with vibrant orange trees,
abundantly filled with reeds, lemons, and pomegranates; (11)
where the wind-swayed kaṅkola vines seemed to dance a hallīsaka dance,
a veritable abode of playful dancing with the delicate grace of lavalī creepers; (12)
as if beckoning weary travelers to rest
by gestures of gently swaying leaves of camphor-banana plants; (13)
as if, like an eminent man, with sprout-like fingers of punnāga branches
gently touching the breast-like cluster of trembling jasmine flowers; (14)
revealing its impassioned heart with split pomegranates,
as if embracing the mādhavī creeper in the form of a husband in the woods; (15)
with sky-reaching cluster fig trees garlanded with countless fruits,
resembling the serpent Ananta bearing millions of cosmic eggs on every side; (16)
covered with jackfruit trees resembling forest snouts, parrot-beaked trees, and palāśa trees,
as if shedding their leaves out of sympathy for separated lovers starved of food; (17)
as if bristling with goosebumps upon seeing the nīpa trees that rival the kadamba...
shining on all sides with clusters of kadamba trees,
adorned with nameru trees like the high peaks of Meru,
and with rājādana and madana trees, as if with the dwellings of lovers,
covered on every slope with lofty cloth-like tents formed by dense banyan trees,
resplendent with clusters of kuṭaja blossoms, as if occupied by herons,
with karamarda, karīra, karaja, and karambaka plants,
shining like the thousand-rayed [sun] with its hands extended toward suppliants,
as if lustrated with lamps by blazing campaka buds,
and surpassing the beauty of lotus ponds with flowering silk-cotton trees,
in some places with tall pīpal trees, in others with golden ketaka blossoms,
and adorned here and there with kṛtamāla and naktamāla trees,
beautified with karkandhu, bandhujīva, and putrajīva trees,
with tinduka, ingudī, and karuṇa trees—an abode of compassion— / as if constantly worshipping Hara, who bears the form of the earth,
with pearls dropped from his own hands in the form of falling madhūka blossoms,
as if fanned by fans with sarja, arjuna, añjana, and bījaka trees,
as if holding up an umbrella in the sky with coconut and date palms,
with abundant neem trees, with mandāras and kovidāras,
with pāṭalā, tamarind, ghoṇṭā, śākhoṭa, and karahāṭaka trees,
with tall śehuṇḍas, castors, and guḍapuṣpas,
and with bakula and tilaka trees, its summit marked as if with a sectarian mark,
with akṣa, plakṣa, and śallakī trees, and with deodar and pine trees,
resplendent with trees and creepers that are ever fruit-bearing and ever flowering,
covered with groves of cardamom, cloves, black pepper, and kulañjana,
extolled for its rose-apples, hog-plums, marking-nuts, śelu, and śrīparṇī trees,
delightful with woods of teak and sandalwood, with white sandalwood and red sandalwood,
adorned with groves of myrobalan, karṇikāra, and āmlakī,
overspread with hundreds of grapevines, betel vines, and long-pepper creepers,
fragrant with jasmine, yūthikā, kunda, and madayantī,
adorned with mālatī flowers having swarms of bees hovering about,
like Kṛṣṇa who came under the guise of a black bee to sport many times with the gopīs,
crowded with various herds of wild beasts, resonant with diverse birds,
surrounded everywhere by varied rivers, lakes, streams, and ponds,
inhabited by hosts of various gods who, having abandoned the celestial realms of meager splendour,
had come, as it were, out of a desire for all-around enjoyment,
as if offering water of welcome on all sides with leaves and flowers,
and greeting him from afar, as it were, with the cries of peacocks.
Then, having seen Nārada, who possessed the splendor of a hundred suns / and illuminated the sky in the firmament,
the mountain went forward from afar to meet him.
The darkness in his caves was dispelled by the radiance of the son of Brahmā's body;
seeing him approach, he cast away the darkness of his mind.
His trepidation was born from Brahmā's radiance; he offered virtuous hospitality:
though hard, he cast off [hardness] and truly assumed softness.

4.1.s: dṛṣṭvā mṛdulatāṃ tasya dvairūpyepi sa nāradaḥ ..
4.1.d: दृष्ट्वा मृदुलतां तस्य द्वैरूप्येपि स नारदः ..
4.1.m: Seeing his softness, despite his double nature, Nārada
rejoiced exceedingly; the minds of the virtuous are won over by humble deference.
Seeing one come to his home, whether a venerable elder or not an elder,
he who, not being heavy, displays humility is truly great; the heavy one is not great.
Toward him, though his peak was high, he lowered his neck,
and the mountain, touching the earth with his head, bowed to the great sage.
Raising him up with both hands and greeting him with blessings,
[Nārada] sat upon the seat indicated by him, exalted even beyond the mind.
With curd, honey, clarified butter, water, unbroken wet barley grains, and dūrvā grass,
with sesamum, kuśa grass, and blossoms, he worshipped him with the eightfold offering of water.
Having received the offering of water, seeing that he was tired, [and making him] relieved of fatigue / by massaging his feet and other services,
the mountain, bowing low, then spoke:
“Today, in an instant, the dust [of my passion] has been removed by the dust of your feet,
and internal darkness too has been swiftly removed by the splendor clinging to your body.
Today my prosperity has borne fruit, and today is an auspicious day for me, O sage;
today fruit has been borne by the meritorious deeds performed and accumulated by me long ago.
Today my status as a mountain will become respected by the wielder of the thunderbolt.”
Hearing this, the sage then paused a little, drawing a deep breath.
Again the best of mountains spoke, his mind seized by agitation:
“O brahmin, skilled in every matter, tell me the cause of your sigh. / 49
Is there anything desired in the three worlds that has not been seen by you?
If you have compassion for me here, let it be told; I bow to you. / 4.1.1.50
My difficult roaring [is quieted] by the masses of joy born of your arrival;
it is not enough to speak repeatedly, yet I shall say one thing. / 51
The capacity to bear the earth in Meru and the rest is praised by ancient men
collectively; but I bear the earth all alone. / 52
Himavān, because of Gaurī's fatherhood, because of being the lord of mountains,
and through his kinship with Paśupati, is the only one respected by the good. / 53
Meru is considered worthy of respect somewhere in my opinion, because he is filled with gold, or because his peaks are jewels,
or even because he is the abode of the gods. / 54
Are there not more than a hundred mountains whose sport is sustaining the earth?

4.1.s: iha saṃti satāṃ mānyā mānyāste tu svabhūmiṣu .. ..55 ..
4.1.d: इह संति सतां मान्या मान्यास्ते तु स्वभूमिषु .. ..55 ..
4.1.m: Here they are respected by the good, but they are respected only in their own lands. / 55
Udaya is sustained merely by the mercy of the rising [sun], because of doubt concerning the bodies of the Mandehas;
Niṣadha does not bear medicinal herbs, and Asta too has its light extinguished. / 56
Nīla is a dwelling of indigo; Mandara has dim eyes;
Malaya is filled with impurity, an abode of snakes; Raivata does not understand wealth. / 57
Those beginning with Hemakūṭa and Trikūṭa have the word kūṭa ['falsehood' or 'peak'] at the end;
those beginning with Kiṣkindha, Krauñca, and Sahya are unable to endure the burden of the earth. / 58 /”
Hearing these words of Vindhya, Nārada thought in his heart:
“Contact with enormous pride does not lead to greatness. / 59
Are there not mountains here possessing spotless splendor, beginning with Śrīśaila,
the mere sight of whose peaks leads to the liberation of the good? / 4.1.1.60
Having reflected, 'Today his strength must be seen,' the sage said:
“Indeed, what you have spoken is true as you disclose the strength of the mountains. / 61
Yet among the mountains, Meru, the lord of mountains, despises you.
It was this that I sighed about, and now it has been disclosed to you. / 62

4.1.s: athavā madvidhānāṃ hi keyaṃ ciṃtā mahātmanām ..
4.1.d: अथवा मद्विधानां हि केयं चिंता महात्मनाम् ..
4.1.m: Or rather, what concern is this to great-souled persons like me?”
Saying, “May it be well with you,” he went along the path of the sky. / 63
When the sage had gone, with an exceedingly agitated mind he blamed himself;
Vindhya, his desires rendered futile, fell into great anxiety. / 64
Vindhya said:
“Fie on the life of one devoid of the arts and sciences! Fie on the life of one devoid of exertion!
Fie on the life of one defeated by a kinsman! Fie on the life of one whose desires are frustrated! / 65

4.1.s: kathaṃ bhunakti sa divā kathaṃ rātrau svapityaho ..
4.1.d: कथं भुनक्ति स दिवा कथं रात्रौ स्वपित्यहो ..
4.1.m: How does he eat by day, alas, how does he sleep at night?

4.1.s: rahaḥ śarma kathaṃ tasya yasyābhibhavanaṃ ripoḥ .. 66 ..
4.1.d: रहः शर्म कथं तस्य यस्याभिभवनं रिपोः .. 66 ..
4.1.m: How can there be secret joy for him whose humiliation comes from an enemy? / 66
Ah, the scorching heat of a forest fire does not torment me so
as the continuous burning of anxiety torments my mind! / 67
It was rightly said by the knowers of antiquity: the form of anxiety is very cruel;
it is not alleviated by medicines, nor by fasting, nor by any other means. / 68
The fever of anxiety steals away men's hunger, sleep, and strength,

4.1.s: rūpamutsāhabuddhiṃ śrī jīvitaṃ ca na saṃśayaḥ .. 69 ..
4.1.d: रूपमुत्साहबुद्धिं श्री जीवितं च न संशयः .. 69 ..
4.1.m: their beauty, enthusiasm, intellect, fortune, and life, without a doubt. / 69
When six days have passed, a fever here is called a chronic fever;
this fierce fever of anxiety becomes fresh day after day. / 4.1.1.70
The blessed Dhanvantari is not here, nor does Caraka wander here;
even the two Nāsatyas are not effective here against this fever of anxiety. / 71

4.1.s: kiṃ karomi kva gacchāmi kathaṃ meruṃ jayāmyaham ..
4.1.d: किं करोमि क्व गच्छामि कथं मेरुं जयाम्यहम् ..
4.1.m: What shall I do? Where shall I go? How shall I conquer Meru?

4.1.s: utplutya tasya śirasi patāmi na patāmyataḥ .. 72 ..
4.1.d: उत्प्लुत्य तस्य शिरसि पतामि न पताम्यतः .. 72 ..
4.1.m: Shall I leap up and fall upon his head? I cannot fall [upon it] from here. / 72
Formerly, when someone of our lineage angered Śakra,
he was stripped of wings; fie on the exertion of one who is wingless! / 73

4.1.s: athavā sa kathaṃ merustathoccaiḥ sparddhate mayā ..
4.1.d: अथवा स कथं मेरुस्तथोच्चैः स्पर्द्धते मया ..
4.1.m: Or else, how can that Meru rival me so proudly?
Those who bear the burden of the earth generally become the grounds of delusion. / 74
Or how could falsehood be imagined in Nārada,
a celibate student, a knower of the Vedas, a resident of Satyaloka? / 75
Is deliberation on what is proper and improper suitable for someone like me?
The mind of those powerless in acts of valor plunges into deliberation. / 76
Or rather, what is the use of these futile anxieties? To the Creator of the universe,

4.1.s: viśveśaṃ śaraṇaṃ yāyāṃ same buddhiṃ pradāsyati .. 77..
4.1.d: विश्वेशं शरणं यायां समे बुद्धिं प्रदास्यति .. 77..
4.1.m: the Lord of the Universe, I shall go for refuge; he will grant me wisdom. / 77
For Viśvanātha is praised as the protector of all the lordless.
Having reflected in his mind for a moment: "It must doubtlessly be so.
I shall do just this; delay of time is not desirable.
A rival and a disease that are growing must not be neglected by the wise.
The sun circumambulates Meru daily indeed,
together with the host of planets and lunar mansions, surely considering him superior in strength."
Having so resolved, the Vindhya mountain, his sight set on battle, grew tall
with peaks that seemed to reach the very end of the boundless sky.
Hostility should never be engaged with anyone, by any person anywhere;
but if it must be done, [it should be done] with effort, so that people do not mock.
Having blocked the sun’s path, the king of mountains felt as though he had achieved his purpose;
he remained at ease, for the future of living beings is subject to fate.
[He thought:] "Whomsoever this creator of restraint curbs today, he will proceed southwards.

4.1.s: sakulīnaḥ sa ca śrīmānsamahānmahitaḥ sa ca .. 84 ..
4.1.d: सकुलीनः स च श्रीमान्समहान्महितः स च .. 84 ..
4.1.m: He of noble birth, he of fortune, he who is great—he too is honored.

4.1.s: yāvatsvaśa ktiṃ śaktopi na darśayati karhicit ..
4.1.d: यावत्स्वश क्तिं शक्तोपि न दर्शयति कर्हिचित् ..
4.1.m: As long as one, though capable, never displays his own power,

4.1.s: tāvatsa laṃghyaḥ sarveṣāṃ jvalano dārugo yathā .. 85 ..
4.1.d: तावत्स लंघ्यः सर्वेषां ज्वलनो दारुगो यथा .. 85 ..
4.1.m: so long can he be transgressed by all, like fire concealed in wood."

Sūta said:
"O Lord, ruler of the past and future, great treasury of all knowledge,
having reached Kāśī, what did the gods do? Tell [me], O infallible one! (1)
Having studied this divine narrative, I do not attain satisfaction.
How was Agasti, the treasure-trove of austerities, petitioned by the gods? (2)
How did even the Vindhya, so lofty, return to its own natural state?
My mind is eager to bathe in the nectar-ocean of your speech." (3)
Having heard this entirely, the sage Vyāsa, son of Parāśara,
began to speak to his faithful disciple. (4)
The son of Parāśara said:
"Listen, O Sūta of great intellect, endowed with devotion and faith!
Let these boys also listen, beginning with Śuka and Vaiśampāyana. (5)
Then, having reached Vārāṇasī, the gods along with the great seers,
without delay, first of all at Maṇikarṇikā, in accordance with the injunctions, (6)
having immersed themselves together with their garments, then having performed the proper rites such as the twilight devotions,
having gratified the ancestors and others who are to be gratified with water containing kuśa grass, scents, and sesamum, (7)
and having gratified each and every one of those who dwell at the sacred ford
with jewels, gold, garments, horses, ornaments, and cows, (8)
and likewise with manifold vessels made of gold, silver, and other [materials],
with cooked foods sweet as nectar and rice cooked in milk with sugar, (9)
with dairy products, gifts of cooked food, gifts of grain in many ways,
with perfumes, sandal, camphor, betel, and charming chowries, (10)
with soft couches with cotton pillows, lamps, mirrors, and seats,
with litters, male and female servants, aerial chariots, cattle, and houses, (11)
with colourful flags and banners, and canopies beautiful as the moon,
and with the provision of annual maintenance along with household furnishings; (12)
and [they gratified] ascetics and practitioners of austerities with shoes and sandals,
with fitting silk cloth and fine garments, and with diverse colourful blankets, (13)
with staffs equipped with waterpots, with deer-skins,
with loincloths, high couches, and attendants and gold; (14)
with monasteries, with food for students, with great wealth for hospitality, (15)

4.3.m: Is it truly the submarine fire itself performing austerity in bodily form, / as motionless as a pillar, pure like the mind of the virtuous? / Or rather, having resorted to this brahminical body, do all splendors / cultivate the supreme abode to attain the state of absolute peace? / The sun burns intensely, and the fire itself is scorched, / through whose fierce austerity even the flickering [lightning] has become steady to this day! / In whose hermitage even beasts of prey are seen all around, / their forms turned gentle, having abandoned their inborn enmity: / The elephant fearlessly scratches the lion with its trunk; / the lion with its noble mane sleeps in the lap of the śarabha; / the boar, though his bristles stand on end, having left his herd, / moves about amidst the wild dogs, his gaze fixed on mustā grass, full of strength; / even the boar does not root up the earth as he does elsewhere, / restrained by fear because all of Kāśī is made of the liṅga; / taking a young pig onto its lap, oh, the hyena fondles it; / brushing aside the tiger cubs, a young fawn, / wagging its tail, drinks with frothy mouth from the tigress; / while a hairy bear sleeps, a monkey with restless fingers / seeks out lice again and again and eats them with the tips of his teeth; / the troop-leading baboons, black-bodied with red faces, / abandon the enmity natural to their species and disport together in one place; / hares frolic with wolves, continually rolling over their backs; / a mouse, its face twitching, scratches the ear of the cat; / curled in the train of a peacock's tail, a cat sleeps most peacefully; / a serpent rubs its throat against the throat of a peacock; / leaping and springing playfully, the mongoose rolls / on the back of the serpent's hood, abandoning the enmity natural to its race; / seeing a mouse moving right before its mouth, / the serpent, though blinded by hunger, does not seize it, nor does the mouse fear it;

4.4.m: Sūta said: / “When questioned by the sage then, O venerable one, what did the gods say? / Speak of that, O great sage, for the welfare of the whole world.” // Śrī Vyāsa said: / Having heard Agastya's words preceded by great respect, / the gods looked toward the face of the lord of intelligence. // The lord of speech [Bṛhaspati] said: / “Listen, O highly fortunate Agastya, to the reason for the gods' arrival. / You are blessed, your purpose is accomplished, and you are venerable even to the great. // Are there not ascetics in every hermitage, on every mountain, in every forest, / O best of sages? Yet your state is quite unique. // The glory of austerity is present here in you; brahminic splendour is firmly established in you; / the supreme glory of merit is in you, generosity is in you, and [greatness of] mind is in you. // This auspicious, faithful wife Lopāmudrā is your partner in religious duties, / equal to the shadow of your body, whose tale brings merit. // Among devoted wives—such as Arundhatī, Sāvitrī, and Anasūyā, / Śāṇḍilyā, Satī, Lakṣmī, Śatarūpā, // Menā, Sunīti, Saṃjñā, and also Svāhā— / just as she is celebrated as the best, none other is, undoubtedly. // When you have eaten, O sage, she eats; when you stand, she stands; / she sleeps after you fall asleep, and wakes before [you]. // She never shows herself to you unadorned; / when you have gone abroad for some task, she is entirely devoid of adornments. // She would not utter your name, for the increase of your lifespan; / nor does she ever utter the name of another man. // Even when reviled, she does not revile in return; even when struck, she remains pleased; / and she says: ‘Master, consider that done which you say: “Do this.”’ // When called, she leaves her household duties and goes swiftly, [saying,] / ‘For what purpose was I called, Lord? Grant your gracious favour.’ // She does not linger long in the doorway, nor does she frequent the doorway; / without having been instructed by you, she gives nothing to anyone. // Unasked, she procures on her own all the articles for worship:

/ wherever her husband takes delight, therein she is always loving. // This alone is the vow of women; this alone is their supreme virtue.”

This alone is the worship of the gods: she should not transgress her husband's word. / Whether he is impotent, in misery, diseased, or even old,
prosperous or destitute, she should never transgress her husband alone. / Always rejoicing when he is pleased, downcast when her beloved is downcast,
she, the virtuous woman, should be of one uniform nature both in prosperity and in adversity. / Even upon the exhaustion of clarified butter, salt, oil, and the like, a devoted wife
should not say to her husband, 'There is none,' nor should she burden him with hardships. / A woman desirous of bathing in sacred waters should drink the water that washed her husband's feet;
far beyond even Śaṃkara or Viṣṇu, her husband alone is superior for a woman. / She who undertakes vows, fasts, and observances by transgressing her husband
steals the life span of her husband, and when dead, goes to hell. / The woman who, prone to anger, retorts back when spoken to,
is born as a bitch in a village or a female jackal in a deserted forest. / For of women this one supreme observance is declared:
having worshipped the feet of her husband, she should eat with firm resolve. / She should not sit upon an elevated seat, nor should she frequent the houses of strangers;
words that cause shame are never to be spoken [by her].
Slander must not be uttered; dispute she should shun from afar. / In the presence of elders she should never speak loudly or laugh.
The foolish woman who, abandoning her husband, wanders about in secret, / is born as a cruel female owl living in a hollow of a tree.
If, when struck, she desires to strike back, she becomes a tigress or a female cat; / and she who casts sidelong glances at another man becomes squint-eyed.
She who, abandoning her husband, eats sweet foods alone, / becomes an inhabitant of a village, a bat feeding on canine feces.
She who, snorting 'humph,' speaks an unpleasant word, indeed becomes dumb; / she who is constantly envious of a co-wife becomes wretched time and time again.
She who, disregarding the sight of her husband, looks at someone else, / becomes one-eyed, averted of face, and deformed.

Seeing him arriving from outside, she should swiftly attend him with water and food, / with betel, fans, foot-massages, and the like;
likewise, with pleasing words and supreme removers of weariness, / she who gratifies her beloved with joy has gratified the three worlds.
A father gives in limited measure, a brother gives in limited measure, a son gives in limited measure; / but a husband is the giver of the boundless—she should always worship him.
The husband is a deity, the husband is a teacher, the husband is dharma, sacred fords, and observances; / therefore, abandoning everything, she should venerate her husband alone.
Just as a body bereft of life goes to impurity in an instant, / so a woman bereft of a husband, even though well-bathed, is ever impure.
Of all inauspicious things, a widow is bereft of auspiciousness; / from the sight of a widow, success is never attained anywhere at any time.
Leaving aside one's mother alone, who is devoid of all auspiciousness, / a wise man should shun even her blessing as though it were a venomous snake.
At the time of a maiden's wedding, the twice-born should recite this: / 'Be the companion of your husband whether he is alive or departed.'
A husband must always be followed by a woman like a shadow by a body, / as the moon by moonlight, as a cloud by lightning.
She who gladly follows her husband from the house to the cemetery / undoubtedly attains the fruit of an aśvamedha at every step.
Just as a snake-catcher forcefully pulls out a snake from a hole, / so a virtuous wife, snatching her husband from the messengers, leads him to heaven.
The messengers of Yama flee far away seeing a virtuous wife, / releasing her husband even if he has committed wicked deeds.
'We messengers are not so afraid of fire, nor are we so afraid of lightning, / as when seeing a devoted wife swooping down.'
The sun burns intensely, and even fire is scorched; / all splendors tremble upon seeing the majesty of devotion to a husband.

rejoicing with her husband, the devoted wife enjoys heavenly bliss.
Blessed is that mother in the world, blessed again is that father, / and blessed is that glorious husband in whose house there is a devoted wife.
Three lineages of the father, three of the mother, and three of the husband— / by the merit of a devoted wife, they enjoy the pleasures of heaven.
Misbehaved women, by the destruction of good conduct, drag down the three lineages— / of father, mother, and husband—and become sorrowful here and in the hereafter.
Wherever the foot of a devoted wife touches the earth, / there the earth considers: 'Here, the purifying woman leaves no burden [upon me].'
Even the sun, fearing, touches the devoted wife; / the moon and the wind also [touch her] only for their own purification, not otherwise.
The waters ever desire the touch of a devoted wife: / 'Today our dullness is destroyed; today we have become the purifiers of others.'
Are there not women in every house, proud of their form and charm? / But a devoted wife is obtained only through devotion to the Lord of the Universe.
A wife is the root of the householder; a wife is the root of happiness; / a wife yields the fruits of dharma; a wife is for the increase of offspring.
The next world and this world—both are won by a wife; / a wifeless man is not fit for the rites of gods, ancestors, guests, and sacrifices.
He indeed should be known as a householder in whose house is a devoted wife; / another woman devours him at every step like an ogress or old age.
Just as the body becomes purified by immersion in the Gaṅgā, / so one becomes purified by the auspicious sight of a devoted wife.
If by fate she somehow does not follow her husband [in death], / even then her good conduct must be preserved; by the breach of good conduct she falls low.
Through her fault, her husband also falls from heaven, not otherwise; / [and likewise] her father, mother, and group of brothers.
And that woman who, upon her husband's death, observes widowhood with restraint, / having attained her husband once again, enjoys the delights of heaven.

4.4.m:
The braid of a widow's hair leads to the binding of her husband; / therefore, a widow should always shave her head. // 74
She should always take only one meal [a day], never a second; / or she should observe a fast of three nights, five nights, or a fortnight, // 75
or she should undertake a fast for a month, or perform the cāndrāyaṇa; / or she should perform the severe kṛcchra, or the taptakṛcchra. // 76
With barley foods, with a diet of fruits, with a diet of vegetables, or with diets restricted to milk, / she should sustain life until her life-breath departs of its own accord. // 77
A woman who sleeps on a bedstead, being a widow, brings about her husband's downfall; / therefore, she should sleep on the bare ground with the desire for her husband's welfare. // 78
Nor should anointing the body be done at any time by a widowed woman; / further, application of fragrant substances should never be done by her. // 79
Each day she must offer water libations to her husband with kuśa grass, sesame, and water, / and likewise to his father and his grandfather, reciting their name and gotra. // 80
Moreover, the worship of Viṣṇu should be performed with the contemplation that he is her husband, and not otherwise; / she should constantly meditate on her husband alone as Hari bearing the form of Viṣṇu. // 81
Whatever is most cherished in the world and whatever was desired by her husband, / that she should bestow upon a virtuous man, desiring to please her husband. // 82
In the months of Vaiśākha, Kārttika, and Māgha, she should observe special vows: / ritual ablution, giving of gifts, pilgrimage to sacred fords, and repeated recitation of Viṣṇu's name. // 83
Water pitchers in Vaiśākha, lamps of clarified butter in Kārttika, / and offerings of grain and sesame in Māgha are celebrated as leading to heaven. // 84
A water shed should be set up in Vaiśākha, and a dripping water-pot offered to the god; / shoes, a fan, an umbrella, fine garments, sandalwood paste, // 85
betel with camphor, as well as the gift of flowers, / many water-vessels, and houses decorated with flowers, // 86
various drinks, and fruits such as grapes and plantains / should be given to the foremost of brahmins, saying, “May my husband be pleased.” // 87
In the month of Ūrja, she should eat barley food, or only one meal a day.

She should avoid eggplant, sūraṇa yam, and velvet bean. // 88
In Kārttika she should avoid oil, in Kārttika she should avoid honey, / in Kārttika she should avoid bell-metal, and in Kārttika she should avoid fermented food. // 89
During a vow of silence in Kārttika, she should present a beautiful bell; / if she has vowed to eat from leaves, she presents a bell-metal vessel filled with clarified butter. // 90
Under the vow of sleeping on the ground, a smooth bed with a mattress should be given; / upon abstaining from fruits, fruit should be given; upon abstaining from flavors, that flavor; // 91
upon abstaining from grain, that grain—or else fine rice is prescribed; / she should diligently give milk-cows adorned with ornaments and gold. // 92
All gifts on one side, and the gift of a lamp on the other: / [all gifts] do not equal a sixteenth part of the gift of a lamp in Kārttika. // 93
When the sun has slightly risen, she should perform the Māgha ritual ablution; / and one who performs the Māgha ritual ablution should undertake religious observances according to her ability. // 94
She should feed brahmins, ascetics, and practitioners of austerities with cooked foods: / with laḍḍukas, pheṇikās, vaṭakas, iṇḍarikās, and the like, // 95
cooked in clarified butter, seasoned with pepper, perfumed with pure camphor, / filled inside with sugar, pleasing to the eyes, and fragrant. // 96
She should also give loads of dry firewood to dispel the cold, / a bodice stuffed with cotton, a soft mattress, and a fine sacred thread, // 97
garments dyed with madder, and cotton cloths, / and many betel leaves with nutmeg and cloves, // 98
variegated blankets, rooms free of drafts, / soft footwear, and fragrant unguents, // 99
preceded by great ritual ablutions, with worship using clarified butter and blankets, / with incenses such as black agallochum burnt in the inner sanctum, // 100
with lamps of thick wicks, and likewise with diverse offerings of food; / and she should say, “May the Lord, who is the true form of my husband, be pleased.” // 1
With such various vows and observances, a widow / should thus spend the months of Vaiśākha, Kārttika, and Māgha. // 2

She must not mount an ox even if her life-breath has reached her throat; / she should not wear a bodice, nor put on any dyed garment. // 3
Devoted to her husband, she should do nothing without asking her sons. / Ever intent on such conduct, even a widow is considered auspicious. // 4
